content.title: Response to Reviewer NkVB
content.comment:
Although we have decided to withdraw this paper, we would like to provide some responses to solve the confusion.

We have discussed [R3] in our Discussion section as a concurrent work since our benchmark and codebase were actually released earlier. Two of the works you referred actually cited our paper in their main part. For example, more than half of the corruption types in [R4] are forked from our codebase and they acknowledged that in their paper. We will have a more thorough discussion in our future version, but we worry that there will be a citation loop because they built upon our work.

We do believe that any corruption or OOD robustness/generalization benchmark should maintain the original semantics of the data. Otherwise, if it is impossible for human beings to recognize the object, machine learning models should not recognize the object, either. All datasets including ImageNet-A, -C, and -R have followed this principle, i.e., it is still possible for humans to recognize the object in the image.  

We will work hard to solve other concerns from the reviewer and contribute to the community, but we indeed believe rigorous benchmarking is essential and will let us reflect on the actual progress in this area.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This work studies 3D point cloud classification robustness.  Firstly, it proposes the ModelNet40-C dataset with 15 types of corruption with 5 severities each.  Then, it benchmarks previous classification SOTA methods on ModelNet40-C.  Surprisingly, previous methods could not generate good performance.  Afterward, it utilizes various augmentation and test-time adaptations with the proposed RobustNet to achieve better classification than previous SOTA methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. It is interesting to study point cloud classification robustness, and it is important to reveal that existing methods could be saturated on the ModelNet data.

2. The proposed RobustNet achieves better results than the previous SoTA on the proposed ModelNet40-C.

Weaknesses:
1. My major concern lies in the definitions of all the "common corruptions''.  First of all, the defined 3 corruption categories are controversial and confusing.  For example, why "cutout" should belong to the "density" category rather than "noise", and why "upsampling" should belong to "noise" rather than "density". Also, what are the differences between the two categories "density" and "noise"?


2. I realize that quite a few selected “common corruptions” are not very frequently used in previous point cloud research works, and therefore it is not straightforward to understand the intuitions behind the design choices.  
    
    2-1). For example, in the “Density” category, why should we consider “Local_Density_Inc” and “Local_Density_Dec”? Do they have any analogous real-world examples?  Their implementations are also not clear: i.e., how to select the anchor points? And how do sample or upsample those points?

    2-2). In the “Noise” category, when will we meet the “Uniform” and “Impulse” corruptions?  Why “Upsampling” is considered corruption?  The “Background” corruption is far different from real-world cases.
    
    2-3). In the “Transformation” category, I check the reference [70], but did not find the reasons why “Shear” could represent the motion distortion in 3D point clouds.  When will we meet the “FFD” distortion?  I also checked the reference paper [27, 77], but did not find any information related to “RBF” or “Inv_RBF”. Then, why should we consider “RBF” and “Inv_RBF”?


3. Following my concerns in the previous questions, I would like to suggest the authors could validate their effectiveness on real-world noisy point cloud classification benchmarks, such as ScanObjectNN.  It is important to justify that the conclusions based on the experiments from ModelNet40-C could facilitate classifying real-captured point clouds.

4. It seems like the proposed RobustNet only slightly outperforms CurveNet.

2. Fig.2 looks kind of blurry, and I suggest improving its visual quality.

3. In Table 1, it is better to explain “AT” in its caption.

4. Table 2 and Table 3 exceed the page margin.
content.summary_of_the_review: In summary, I am worried about the defined corruption, because lots of them seem to be not common.  Also, the intuitions behind those corruptions are not straightforward.  Additionally, I am also worried about its effectiveness on real-world point cloud classification.  Given the above, I could not suggest its acceptance at the current stage, and I am willing to reconsider my rating once the authors' response and the other reviews are available.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
### Summary of the Paper:

This paper introduces a new dataset, ModelNet40-C, to conduct robustness evaluations of point cloud classification models. The ModelNet40-C data are generated by corrupting the point clouds from ModelNet40. There are 15 corruption types in ModelNet40-C, mainly from three corruption patterns: density, noise, and transformation. On top of this test set, the authors benchmarked 9 representative
point cloud classification models and compared their robustness. Based on the results, the authors empirically made several conclusions and discussed some possible solutions for designing robust network architecture and augmentation techniques. Besides, the authors proposed RobustNet and PointCutMixup, by combining several useful components from existing works. The effectiveness of these two contributions is verified and compared with other methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strength:

1. The design of corruption types in ModelNet40-C is comprehensive. The authors considered 15 different corruptions from various perspectives. Also, the different severity levels for each corruption are included and tested in detail.

2. The experiment settings and results are systematic and thorough. The authors must spend quite some effort in designing and evaluating the robustness across different point cloud classification models.

3. The benchmark and codebase are somewhat complete. Projects with detailed benchmarks and evaluations are always beneficial for the general community.


### Weaknesses:

1. **Limited literature review and novelty**. Although the authors are claiming that *"ModelNet40-C will serve as a first step towards 3D point cloud corruption-resistant models"*, there actually exist several works in the field of out-of-distribution robustness probing of point clouds. For example, [R1], [R2], [R3], [R4], [R5], and [R6]. Among them, [R3] and [R5] are highly relevant since they also tackle corruptions upon the ModelNet40 dataset. It is strange that the authors mainly highlight the adversarial-based methods in Sec. 2 (which are less relevant to this work) while ignoring the already mature literature from the 3D common corruption side.

2. **Motivations that are not clear enough**. The authors are emphasizing throughout the paper that they are *``preserving the original semantics of point clouds"*. This motivation, however, is inconsistent with the objective of corruption; recall from ImageNet-C / ImageNet-R that the motivation for creating corruption is to simulate the out-of-training-distribution scenarios that tend to happen during inference time in the real world. Such corruptions, in a sense, do not need semantic preservation. Besides, it is hard to judge whether or not each of the 15 proposed corruptions is a reasonable design and should be included in the benchmark.

3. **Limited technical contributions**. The authors further proposed two components, i.e., RobustNet and PointCutMixup. These two contributions, however, are a bit trivial in the sense that: 1) they are just a simple ensemble of existing methods; and 2) their performance is not significant (e.g., Table 4, Table 5, and Table 6).

4. **Nonnegligible typos and grammatical issues**. There are notable typos and grammatical errors throughout the current version of this paper, which are hurting the readability. A thorough proofreading is a must during the revision.

5. **Illustrations that require improvements**. Some of the figures in the main body as well as the supplementary pages (i.e., from page 15 to page 26) are of low quality in terms of visibility and readability.

### References:
- [R1] "[3D Common Corruptions and Data Augmentation](https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2022/papers/Kar_3D_Common_Corruptions_and_Data_Augmentation_CVPR_2022_paper.pdf)," CVPR, 2022.
- [R2] "[3D Common Corruptions for Object Recognition](https://openreview.net/pdf?id=Evar7nqAQtL)," ICMLW, 2022.
- [R3] "[Benchmarking and Analyzing Point Cloud Classification under Corruptions](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2202.03377.pdf)," ICML, 2022.
- [R4] "[Common Corruption Robustness of Point Cloud Detectors: Benchmark and Enhancement](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2210.05896.pdf)," arXiv, 2022.
- [R5] "[Unsupervised Representation Learning for 3D Point Cloud Data](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2110.06632.pdf)," arXiv, 2022.
- [R6] "[Benchmarking the Robustness of LiDAR-Camera Fusion for 3D Object Detection](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2205.14951.pdf)," arXiv, 2022.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
### Clarity:

The main motivation of this paper, although might not be correct in a sense, is somewhat interesting. However, the descriptions of some technical details are not clear enough. More importantly, the literature review is extremely limited and quite some of the most relevant works are not discussed in the current version of this paper.

### Quality:

The experiment part of this paper does contribute several interesting findings; while the overall writing and the illustrations, such as figures and tables, need further improvements.

### Novelty:

The motivation for probing the out-of-training-distribution robustness for point cloud classification models is interesting. However, there have existed notably prior works that have already touched this field (see Weakness 1). Since the authors are not directly discussing or comparing their methods to existing ones, the novelty of this work is somehow questionable.

### Reproducibility:

The authors have included their codebase, which seems reliable. However, I didn't go through all the details of their provided code.
content.summary_of_the_review:
### Summary of the Review:

This review evaluates the motivation, novelty, and other factors of this paper, mainly from the following perspectives:

- The motivation for probing 3D robustness is interesting, but this work does not exhibit notable superiority in this direction. Especially when compared with some recent 3D common corruptions as mentioned in Weakness 1.
- The benchmarking and evaluation parts of this work are its strength, which should be somewhat useful for researchers in the areas of point cloud recognition, out-of-distribution detection, robustness, etc.
- The technical contribution of this work is limited, meaning that the introduced RobustNet and PointCutMixup only bring trivial improvements while their original ideas are stemming from existing papers.
- The presentation and illustrations of the current version of this paper need further improvements.

In summary, this work has noticeable advantages as well as drawbacks. The current version of this paper needs further improvements and enhancements.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper contributes a new dataset constructed from the well-known ModelNet40 dataset (object-level point cloud data). The new dataset ModelNet40-C consists of 15 common and realistic corruptions and can be used to evaluate the robustness of the point cloud network. Apart from the built dataset, this paper also evaluates the robustness of previous point cloud networks, like PointNet, PointNet++, DGCNN, PoointMLP, etc, and provides some insights about the robustness, such as how corruptions impact the performance, how the networks are affected by the corruptions, and how the augmentations improve the performance. Based on the dataset and the insights, this paper develops a new network, RobustNet, and an augmentation technique, PointCutMixup to improve the robustness.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
=== Strength ===

- This paper is well-written and easy to follow. The code is also provided, which I believe benefits the reproducibility and future research.

- The constructed dataset is helpful to design a more robust point cloud network and improve the robustness of previous methods. I think the dataset is beneficial for the community.

- I like the organization of the work, i.e., introduce the constructed dataset -> evaluate previous methods and give some insights -> provide a new solution.

=== Weaknesses === 

- I am curious about whether previous point cloud operations are implemented in a common architecture. In detail, as far as I know, previous networks generally have different structures, such as different channels, different depths, and different decoders. Therefore, if those methods are evaluated in different structures, I doubt the preciseness of the insights and conclusions. 

- Following the above comment, I wonder if the structures are changed, such as more channels or more layers, whether the insights still hold true.

- Some SOTA methods are not evaluated. Currently, Transformer-based methods have achieved very high performance for point cloud analysis, like Point Transformer [1] and Stratified Transformer [2]. Although the results on PCT have been reported, more evaluations are expected.

- While the developed RobustNet is somehow incremental, it is built based on the insights, and I think it is acceptable. However, an analysis of the modules should be provided, i.e., the ablations.

- other suggestions: I would like to see how the dataset improves the robustness. For example, if we pretrain the point cloud network on the dataset via self-supervised learning, is the robustness improved? 


[1] Zhao et al., Point Transformer.

[2] Lai et al., Stratified Transformer for 3D Point Cloud Segmentation.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper is about a benchmark/dataset for point cloud classification and its robustness to point cloud corruptions. This paper proposes the ModelNet40-C dataset, based on the ModelNet40 dataset, and the authors evaluate multiple neural networks used for point cloud classification and note that under corruptions, performance degrades significantly.

The paper also proposes a new point cloud processing network, RobustNet, a combination of network designs proven to be robust in previous results in the paper, and results show that it improves robustness on ModelNet40-C. Additionally PointCutMixup is a new data augmentation technique meant to increase robustness, by combining three candidate point clouds in a mixup fashion, with also a slight improvement in robustness.

The contributions are:
- A dataset/benchmark, ModelNet40-C, designed to test 15 corruptions at 5 different severity levels.
- Important insights on the interaction between model architectures and corruption types. These insights can lead future research into more robust network architectures for point cloud processing. In particular different network architectures have varying degrees of robustness to different corruptions.
- Additional insights between different corruption types and data augmentation/adaptation methods, showing that some data augmentation/adaptation methods perform well in some corruptions while failing to others. There is no single size fits all solution for this problem.
- This paper also proposes RobustNet whcih combines robust network design into a single network, being new state of the art for robust point cloud classification on ModelNet40-C.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
- This is a good contribution, robustness to corruptions in point cloud processing is not usually explored, the PointNet paper did explore some corruptions but it was a very basic experiment, this paper greatly expands this concept into a full benchmark.
- The benchmark covers a good set of point cloud processing neural networks, ensuring robust conclusions and insights.
- The ModelNet40-C dataset covers a very good set of corruptions (15 different types), and the paper defines a categorization for these corruptions, as well as allowing for 5 different corruption severities.
- The paper's evaluation allows for many relevant insights and relationships between the proposed corruptions, point cloud network design, and data augmentation or robustness methods.
- In particular there are some very interesting insights: labels for the corruptions allow to distinguish how different models are affected by different corruptions, background corruption seems to heavily affect most models, as well as LiDAR and Occlusion.
- The authors also evaluate data augmentation and adaptation techniques to improve robustness, which overall does improve robustness, but there is no technique that outperforms all others, in particular when considering individual corruptions, again some methods are robust to some corruptions but weak to some other corruptions.
- The paper acknowledges concurrent work (reference 43) that is similar (also about point cloud corruptions and robustness), and makes correct comparisons and shortcomings of previous work, I believe this is very good scientific practice.
- I have no doubts over the evaluation, it looks correct to me. Metrics are simple (basically classification error) but I do not think more metrics would be needed.
- The paper is well presented and written, I have no comments on writing, only some about presentation in weaknesses and minor issues below.

Weaknesses
- In the paper and supplementary, the severity of each corruption is not clearly specified. Section A in the appendix should define these, but only does it in some cases, for example, the Gaussian and Uniform noise have varying variance depending on the severity (which makes sense), but the exact values of the variance/std deviation are not present. Please present something like a table with all severity values and the associated parameters for each corruption.
- Related to the previous point, only the corruptions are presented visually for some sample point clouds, but not the severity of the corruptions, for example in Figure 2, I think it is better to also visually present examples of each corruption along with the five different severities, there is space in the appendix for this.

Minor Issues
- In Table 2, ER_cor is presented in the second column, as an overall error over all corruptions, but the "Validity" paragraph in Section 5.1 refers to ER_c, and sometimes to ER_s,c which is not presented in the Table or plots in Figure 8 and 9, please clarify the notation or label the plots/columns so the reader can follow your argument.
- RobustNet is presented in Sec 6, but it is already present in results in previous sections (for example in Table 2), I think I would define RobustNet in an earlier section, before the experiments.
- RobustNet is detailed in Section B in the appendix, but I think this is too little detail for reproducibility, a diagram of the whole network architecture would be better for understanding and reproducibility. Most papers that define new architectures do this, from where future users will implement your network.
- Many plots in the supplementary (like Fig 8 and 9) do not have axis labels, please add them, the reader should not have to guess the meaning.
- RobustPointSet is discussed in the appendix, but this should go in Section 7 (Discussion and Conclusion), at least briefly.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
To me the paper is clear, it is well written and presented, the results and conclusions are clear. I only have minor remarks and comments about the lack of information about the severity values of each corruption, and sample point clouds for different severity values. With these issues fixed, I think this is a high quality paper.

The paper is high on novelty, as corruptions for point cloud classification have been barely explored, with only two concurrent works that looks similar to this benchmark, and I can confirm that the benchmark proposed in this paper is higher quality than reference 43, the insights and interactions are also very important for future research.

The novelty of this paper is in its contributions, the benchmark and dataset, the insights about interaction between point cloud network design and different corruption types, same interactions with data augmentation and adaptation methods, and the proposed RobustNet that improves performance on the corrupted dataset, as well as the proposed PointCutMixup augmentation.
content.summary_of_the_review:
My recommendation is to accept this paper. This is a high quality benchmark for point cloud corruptions and its effect on models, there is a clear effect that models lose predictive performance on corrupted datasets, but more importantly is that the performance degradation varies with the model architecture, so this paper presents good insights on why this happens, and combines different architectural decisions into a single network (RobustNet) which improves performance on corrupted point clouds, setting a new state of the art.

The paper also explores alternate training methods to increase robustness, in particular adaptability methods and several forms of data augmentation, from where it can be inferred that both kinds of methods improve robustness, but to a different degree and are more/less robust to different kinds of corruptions. From these insights the authors propose a new data augmentation based on mixup, called PointCutMixup.

The paper only has minor issues, mostly related to clarifying  details on corruption severity and notation about metrics.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper presents a comprehensive benchmark, ModelNet40-C,  for 3D point cloud recognition robustness against common corruption. It suggests 15 corruption types consisting of three categories (Noise, Transformation, and Density).
The authors conduct experiments on several SOTA point cloud classification models with existing data augmentation techniques. They further propose RobustNet and PointCutMixup to further enhance corruption robustness.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Pros:

(1) The proposed RobustNet achieves good performance on ModelNet40-C.

(2) The extensive analysis and discussion are conducted on nine representative models with data augmentation and test-time adaption methods.

Cons:

Benchmark:

As there are two existing benchmarks ([43], [56]) for point cloud corruption robustness, the reviewer thinks the novelty of the proposed benchmark is not good enough. Including more datasets on point cloud classification or more tasks (e.g., point cloud segmentation, detection) is better.

Method:

(1) The designs of RobustNet and PointCutMixup are incremental to previous works. 

(2) Why does the RobustNet consist of four transformer layers? There is no insight into this.

Experiments:

(1) It is better to show the relative corruption results, as [21] does, which is a much fairer way to compare the robustness capacity among different models. 

(2) It is suggested to include the standard performances (without corruption) in Table 2, Table 3, and Table 5.

The authors include the code in supplementary material, which make this work reproducible.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a point cloud dataset, a.k.a. ModelNet-C processed from ModelNet, for benchmarking 3D point cloud corruption robustness, including 15  common corruptions. The paper unveils the superiority of Transformer network over SOTA in terms of robustness. Besides, they introduce RobustNet and PointCutMixup for further improving corruption robustness.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Pros:
+) The paper is easy to follow. It is the first 3D point cloud dataset for corruption robustness, which may play a critical role for real-world robust point cloud detection and localization;
+) They show some key insights of what types of corruption affects the classification most, e.g. occlusion, rotation and noises. 
+) They mitigate data augmentation tricks from vision tasks, e.g. ensembling and PointCutMixup, and show performance improvements.

Cons: 
-) A major issue is there was a ICML22 work [1] working on the same problem. The authors need to justify it. 
-) Motivation unclear. It's important to quantify the distortion of real-world corrupted data and provide a more detailed connection of captured real-world data with artificial data and their qualitative and quantitative gap. 
-) Lack of technical novelty. Excluding new data contribution, some details such as CutMixup is not something new. The authors should discuss the main technical novelty of the paper. 
-) A more clear Fig. 1 should be presented, and more visual results of crafted corrupted data. 

Jiawei Ren, et al., [1] Benchmarking and Analyzing Point Cloud Classification under Corruptions, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2202.03377.pdf
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper shows an interesting perspective on benchmarking 3D point cloud robustness, in which they adapt the ModelNet40 into a ModelNet40-C. They have conducted extensive experiments on validating the importance of performing detection tasks on corrupted dataset, and have shown a few insights related to the corrupted data and data augmentation tricks. However, they did not show any real-world correpted data and their connections with crafted data, which is not enough for validating the proposed dataset. Besides, more in-depth analysis of model design, data details and limitation should be further explored. Lastly, a critical renference is missing.

content.title: Benchmarking and Improving Robustness of 3D Point Cloud Recognition against Common Corruptions
content.abstract: Deep neural networks on 3D point cloud data have been widely used in the real world, especially in safety-critical applications. However, their robustness against corruptions is less studied. In this paper, we present ModelNet40-C, a comprehensive benchmark on 3D point cloud corruption robustness, consisting of 15 common and realistic corruptions. Our evaluation shows a significant gap between the performances on ModelNet40 and ModelNet40-C for state-of-the-art models. We identify a number of critical insights for future studies on corruption robustness in point cloud recognition. For instance, we unveil that Transformer-based architectures with proper training recipes achieve the strongest robustness. To bridge this gap, we further propose RobustNet and PointCutMixup that embrace the merits of existing architectural designs to further improve the corruption robustness in the 3D point cloud domain, after evaluating a wide range of augmentation and test-time adaptation strategies. Our codebase and dataset are open-sourced.
